label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
which_first: 03, because in a gap between meetings I want the factory and the four steps in five minutes, and it gives both without a story detour.

03.one_line: Three pages: who is in it, how it runs, how it stops at 18:44, then four steps and a note on running it as a team of several.

10.one_line: Fuller and more convincing on the failures and the loop, but the practical team advice stays one paragraph on page 4 and one step on page 11, and some pages are thin with a dashed figure still to come.

tomorrow: Write one page of rules for my own agent (what it is for, what it may change, when it stops and asks me), then agree with two teammates one shared brief, one board and one named person who may lift the hold; first small shipped thing for the stand the same day, such as the stand's questions page.
would_share: yes, with the two or three colleagues on the conference team who already run their own agents; I would send the 3-page edition, page 5 (the four steps and the team paragraph).
why_buy: It would need a worked team example (who holds the hold, how three people's agents share one board, what a week of it looks like before a deadline) and a do-this-now box per chapter, as page 11 promises. Real cost per person would also help.

best_page.why: The stop at 18:44 with the rule that anyone can stop and only one person restarts, then four concrete steps, the team-of-several note and what it costs. It is all I need to copy the pattern.

worst_page.why: A dashed 'figure to come' box sits at the top, and the interview is fragmentary (Dev, Narrator, Deck, Storyteller in short lines). The freeze lesson is the useful takeaway, but it is buried in one dense paragraph.

one_change_before_the_editor_sees_it: Page 11 of the 10-page edition: add a short worked team example (three people, three agents, one brief, one board, who holds the hold) to step 5, because that is my real use and the team advice is currently one sentence; also fill or remove the 'figure to come' boxes on pages 3, 4, 8 and 9.
notes: The audience line on page 2 says 'for anyone with an idea and no team yet', which is not quite my case: I have a team and agents already. The 10-page version adds 'alone or with others', which helps. The cover is strong. Page 6 of the 3-page edition and page 12 of the 10-page one list repository file paths as sources, which mean nothing to me and read as clutter. Pages 5 and 6 of the 10-page edition lean on in-jokes (the missing @, sheepish) that a newcomer will not get. The shared-hold rule (name who may lift it when its owner is away) is the most useful single idea for a team; it deserves a heading. The dependence on one person who alone restarts the factory is close to my deal-breaker about a central person, though the 'team of several' note softens it.
